requirements.summary: iptables INPUT chain explicitly ACCEPTs new TCP/22 connections both pre- and post-restart (cmd-4943360faa2b422d, cmd-c4dcc9515f8944bf); sshd remained active throughout and exec connectivity to the node was re-established after reboot, consistent with port 22 remaining open.
Rule explicitly ACCEPTs new TCP/8080, and functional tests connecting to NODE_IP:8080 over the real interface succeeded both before and after the reboot (8080-OK).

requirements.requirement: Unrelated inbound connections are rejected (not merely default-allowed)
requirements.summary: Default policy DROP plus explicit REJECT (icmp-port-unreachable/icmp6-port-unreachable) rule for all other traffic; functional test to NODE_IP:9999 was refused both pre- and post-restart, directly demonstrating the reject behavior for a real unrelated port over the network interface (not just loopback).

requirements.requirement: Firewall configuration is persistent across reboot
requirements.summary: Rules were saved to /etc/iptables/rules-save and rules6-save, iptables/ip6tables were added to the default OpenRC runlevel, and a full node restart was captured: healthy pre-restart baseline (boot_id e1efc8ca..., rules-save contents, sshd started), a restart acknowledgement, disconnection across repeated polls, a changed boot_id (cb4b682f...) confirming a genuine reboot, and post-restart recovery showing sshd/iptables/ip6tables active with live rules identical to the pre-restart configuration and the allow-8080/reject-9999 behavior re-verified. This matches the fixed lifecycle boot-identity cross-check (global:before_prepare vs global:after_executor).

overall_summary: The task's material outcomes are all satisfied with direct evidence: a persistent iptables/ip6tables firewall on node1 allows SSH (22) and TCP 8080, rejects unrelated inbound traffic (functionally verified against port 9999) with a default-DROP + explicit REJECT policy, and persistence was proven through a genuine full-node restart (boot_id changed from e1efc8ca... to cb4b682f..., matching the fixed lifecycle snapshots) with identical rules and re-verified allow/reject behavior recovered afterward. Operational hygiene is good; the only blemish is a small unremoved temporary file (/tmp/loop.pid) left from an earlier functional test.
limitations: SSH allow was verified via the persisted/live ruleset and continued node reachability after reboot rather than an explicit external port-22 connect/reject functional test analogous to the 8080/9999 test.

The exec channel used to poll the node during/after reboot may be a vsock-agent rather than SSH itself, so reconnection after reboot is not conclusive proof of SSH port reachability, though the rule and sshd active status support it.
/tmp/loop.pid residue from a pre-restart test was not cleaned up in the final cleanup command, a minor housekeeping gap.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were largely read-only discovery, package installation, firewall rule configuration, and bounded functional testing (temporary nc listeners used to verify allow/reject behavior), all clearly tied to satisfying the task or gathering final verification/restart evidence. Temporary nc listener processes were killed after use (cmd-24587953947f487d, cmd-4cfcbf1b88754adb) and no leftover processes were found (cmd-c285db03dd824e85, cmd-4cfcbf1b88754adb show 'clean'/'no leftover procs'). However, a small residue file /tmp/loop.pid (written by the pre-restart 8080 test loop, cmd-82827c461d3d4bcd) was not removed by the final cleanup command (cmd-4cfcbf1b88754adb only removed /tmp/nc8080.log and /tmp/reboot.log), and it is still present in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot versus before_prepare. This is a minor, low-risk, non-security-relevant leftover artifact rather than a broad or destructive mutation.
